203.section: 2) Maintaining a Safe Following Distance from the Vehicle Ahead
203.body:
2) Maintaining a Safe Following Distance from the Vehicle Ahead

1. While driving, the driver must maintain an appropriate and sufficient distance from the vehicle ahead to be able to stop safely when the vehicle ahead reduces speed.

2. The driver must observe the driving behavior of the vehicle ahead at all times and reduce speed in advance before the vehicle gets too close to the vehicle ahead, which could result in danger.

3) Braking Under Various Conditions

In the event of an emergency caused by various factors, such as the vehicle ahead being involved in an accident or suddenly seeing an obstruction on the road, the driver must remain calm and not panic, hold the handlebars firmly, apply the brakes, and check both side mirrors to determine whether there is sufficient distance from the following vehicle to safely change lanes to avoid the obstruction. If it is possible to do so, control the vehicle to avoid the obstruction, then stop the vehicle in a safe area and report the incident.

4) Decelerating Safely

When reducing speed or decelerating, the driver must not do so suddenly, as the following vehicle may not be able to reduce speed in time, which could result in an accident. The driver must check the rearview mirror and both side mirrors to verify whether the following vehicle has sufficient distance to safely reduce speed accordingly. If there is sufficient distance, tap the brake and release once to warn other following vehicles, then apply the brake to reduce speed as desired.

5) Maintaining a Safe Following Distance from the Vehicle Ahead

The driver must maintain an appropriate distance from the vehicle ahead based on the current speed being used, taking into account emergency situations in which the vehicle ahead may stop suddenly. The driver should observe the positions of other vehicles sharing the road to periodically assess the driving situation.

Maintaining a Safe Distance from Other Vehicles

The distance from the vehicle ahead and behind should be approximately 3 seconds, which can be observed by mentally counting 3 seconds to determine whether the driver reaches the point where the vehicle ahead previously was before the count is complete. If the driver reaches that point before 3 seconds, the distance is too short, and the driver should reduce speed to increase the following distance.

204.body:
**Lateral Distance**

Motorcycle riders should maintain a distance of no less than 1.5 meters from other vehicles to guard against driving errors by those vehicles, which may swerve from side to side. Additionally, if the vehicle alongside is a truck or a large vehicle, the rider will also be affected by the wind force generated by that vehicle.

Furthermore, the method for counting the 3-second interval is for the rider to count mentally: "one thousand one," "one thousand two," "one thousand three."

**6) Proper Use of Brakes**

In cases where it is necessary to stop the vehicle or reduce speed, the rider must use the brakes properly to avoid danger. The rider must use both the front brake and the rear brake together. This is because using only the front brake may cause the rider to be thrown forward, and using only the rear brake may cause the motorcycle to skid and lose balance. When the motorcycle is about to stop, use the left foot to touch the ground to support the motorcycle, and keep the right foot on the foot brake pedal to be ready to apply the brake if the motorcycle skids.

**7) Using Appropriate Speed for the Situation**

When determining speed, motorcycle riders must consider the road environment, including the position and speed of other vehicles, in order to decide on an appropriate speed.

209.body:
• Do not overtake more than one vehicle at a time, as it will make it difficult to change lanes back in the event that there is oncoming traffic or other emergencies.

**8. Use of Traffic Lanes**

• The driver must drive in their own traffic lane. The driver must not straddle the lane dividing line and the road shoulder. Observe the lane dividing lines and shoulder lines visible ahead.

• Drivers of all types of vehicles must drive in the left lane. On roads where lanes in the same direction have been divided into two or more lanes, or where a bus lane has been designated in the leftmost lane, the driver must drive in the leftmost lane or the lane nearest to the bus lane, except in the following cases, where driving on the right side of the road is temporarily permitted:

1. The traffic lane is obstructed or closed to traffic.
2. The road has been designated as a one-way road by a traffic officer.
3. The driver must enter the correct lane when approaching an intersection or junction.
4. When overtaking another vehicle.
5. When the driver is traveling at a speed higher than vehicles in the left lane, for the safety of slower vehicles and to allow faster vehicles to overtake safely.

210.body:
Motorcycles must use the left lane. In the case of overtaking another vehicle, the rider must return to the left lane after safely passing the overtaken vehicle. The rider must not obstruct traffic and must move to the left lane when a faster vehicle is about to overtake.

**3) Changing Lanes**

When changing lanes, the rider must check the distance from other nearby vehicles to avoid collisions by following these steps:

1. Look in the left or right side mirror in the direction you intend to change lanes to check the position of following vehicles.
2. Look over your shoulder to check for vehicles beside you and reduce blind spots.
3. When it is safe, activate the turn signal at least 30 meters before changing lanes.
4. Change lanes with caution.
5. Turn off the turn signal once the vehicle is traveling straight again.

**4) Making a U-Turn**

U-turn points are another location where accidents occur frequently, with many common accident patterns such as rear-end collisions, side collisions with the vehicle making the U-turn, and being struck from the side by a vehicle traveling straight. Therefore, to make a U-turn on the road safely, the rider must follow these steps:

1. Move to the right traffic lane.
2. Activate the right turn signal at least 30 meters before the U-turn point.
3. Reduce speed to an appropriate level for turning to make the U-turn.
4. Control the motorcycle close to the line for ease of turning.
5. Reduce speed and shift to a low gear.
6. Stop the vehicle and check the distance of oncoming vehicles to see how far they are or whether they have stopped to give way to you.
7. When it is safe, move off using a low gear, then gradually increase speed and shift to higher gears.
8. When it is safe, move to the left lane.

211.body:
5) Riding on Curves

• Riding Technique
1. Look ahead toward the curve in advance.
2. Ease off the throttle and reduce speed before reaching the curve; lean the body and adjust according to conditions.

• Be Cautious of Other Vehicles Beyond the Curve
Motorcycle riders must always be aware that when riding on curves, there may be vehicles or other obstructions beyond the curve. Therefore, riders must reduce speed every time to minimize potential dangers.

• Speed – Do Not Exceed the Speed Limit
When riding on curves, riders must use a low speed appropriate to the road conditions, especially the road surface condition. If the surface is slippery, the curve radius is tight, or the road is not banked for the curve, riders must use an even lower speed. This is because high speed may cause the vehicle to slide off the curve, lose control, and result in a severe accident.

• Gear Shifting
Riders should not shift gears while riding through a curve, as it may cause the engine to operate unevenly and result in loss of vehicle control.

• Braking
Riders should brake before reaching the curve. While riding through the curve, do not brake harshly, because harsh braking of the front or rear wheel will cause that wheel to skid, resulting in loss of vehicle control.

• Overtaking
Riders should avoid overtaking while riding in a curve area, as visibility is limited and the rider may be squeezed by cars or trucks.

213.body:
**Riding Posture**

The rider must lean slightly forward while going uphill to shift more weight onto the front wheel, and must lean backward while going downhill to increase the load on the rear wheel for easier balance.

Regarding gear use while riding down steep grades, the following practices should be observed:

When riding downhill or on a slope, use a low gear to utilize engine braking to reduce speed and share the workload of the braking system. This is because using the brakes continuously for an extended period on a downhill slope can cause the braking system to malfunction and may lead to accidents.

**11. Sharing the Road with Other Types of Vehicles (Automobiles and Pedestrians)**

**• Yielding the Right of Way**

When riding on the road together with automobiles and other vehicles, even though motorcycle riders have high maneuverability, they must strictly obey traffic rules and signs as well. They must also yield to vehicles that have the right of way, such as when pulling out of a parking space, a side street (soi), or a U-turn point, etc.

**• Blind Spots**

When riding a motorcycle, the rider must be aware of the limitations of eyesight and side mirrors in seeing other vehicles at certain points, as shown in the illustration.

214.body:
Therefore, the rider must periodically check blind spots by looking over the shoulder with a quick head turn and then turning back to observe the traffic conditions ahead as before. Motorcycle riders must check blind spots every time before pulling out, turning, and changing lanes.

At the same time, motorcycle riders should not ride in positions that are in the blind spots of cars, because car drivers may not see them and may suddenly change lanes, which could result in a sideswipe collision.

**12. Riding as a Motorcycle Passenger**

1) Carrying Passengers
Motorcycle riders must ensure that passengers are properly dressed, wearing a safety helmet, and seated in a safe manner.

2) Number of Pillion Riders
The law stipulates that a motorcycle rider may carry only one passenger.

3) Wearing a Safety Helmet
For safety, the rider must ensure that the passenger wears a safety helmet every time they ride on a motorcycle. The motorcycle rider shall be liable for punishment if the passenger does not wear a safety helmet.

**13. Carrying Goods**

1. When carrying goods in the space behind the rider, care must be taken to prevent items from falling off.
2. The weight of goods carried must not exceed 150 kilograms as prescribed by law.
3. Goods should not be placed in the front basket to the extent that they block the headlight.
4. Items should not be hung on the handlebars, as this can cause problems with steering control while turning.

**14. Techniques for Riding Through Intersections**

1) Entering an Intersection

1. Riding into an intersection
   - The rider must watch out for vehicles traveling on the main road from both the left and right.
   - Activate the right turn signal.
   - Yield to vehicles on the main road first, and wait for a gap with sufficient distance.
   - When pulling out, the rider must shift to a lower gear to provide the engine with more power for acceleration.

215.section: 2. Turning left into a minor road
215.body:
2. Turning left into a minor road
• The rider must activate the left turn signal.
• Consider the curvature of the turn in order to reduce speed appropriately.
• Check the blind spot on the left side.
• Reduce speed and begin controlling the vehicle into the curve.
• Look ahead through the entire curve to prepare for any situations or obstacles that may be behind the curve.
• Maintain a constant speed until riding through the curve.

3. Turning right into a minor road
• The rider must signal a right turn, reduce speed, and ride close to the lane dividing line on the right side.
• Yield to traffic on the main road; the rider should stop at a distance from the center of the intersection to allow other vehicles to turn through safely.
• Wait until there is a sufficient gap in traffic to make the turn, then turn right into the minor road.
• Before turning into the minor road, the rider must check and be certain that there will be no collision with pedestrians crossing the road.

2) Wheel Path of Trucks While Turning
The rear wheels of a truck will track inward toward the inside of the turn. Therefore, motorcyclists must not ride close to the side of a truck that is turning, as they may be sideswiped.

216.body:
**15. Stopping and Parking**

**1) Definitions of Stopping and Parking**

**Parking (Park):** The Road Traffic Act B.E. 2522, Section 54, Chapter 4, Paragraph 2 defines that a driver must park on the left side of the roadway and park with the left side of the vehicle parallel to and close to the road edge or shoulder at a distance of no more than 25 centimeters, or park in the direction or on the side of the roadway designated by the traffic officer. However, in cases where there is a bus lane on the far left of the roadway, drivers are prohibited from parking in such a manner during the designated hours for the use of that bus lane.

**Stopping (Stop):** Section 22 stipulates that a driver must comply with traffic signals or traffic signs appearing ahead. In the case of an amber traffic signal light, the driver shall prepare to stop behind the stop line in order to comply with the signal that will appear next, as stated in (2), except for a driver who has already passed the stop line, who may proceed. In the case of a red traffic signal light or a red traffic sign bearing the word "Stop," the driver shall stop behind the stop line.

Stopping and parking may occur for the following reasons:

- Parking to wait for passengers
- Parking to wait for loading or unloading goods from the vehicle
- Parking due to a problem occurring with the vehicle or the driver

**2) Places Where Stopping Is Prohibited**

1. In a traffic lane, except when stopping close to the left edge of the roadway in cases where there is no bus lane
2. On the sidewalk
3. On a bridge or in a tunnel
4. At an intersection
5. In an area with a no-stopping traffic sign
6. Directly at the entrance or exit of a building or driveway
7. In a safety zone
8. In a manner that obstructs traffic

**3) Places Where Parking Is Prohibited**

1. On the sidewalk
2. On a bridge or in a tunnel
3. At an intersection or within 10 meters of an intersection
4. At a crosswalk or within 3 meters of a crosswalk
5. In an area with a no-parking traffic sign
6. Within 3 meters of a fire hydrant
7. Within 10 meters of a traffic signal installation
8. Within 15 meters of a railway crossing
9. Double-parked alongside another vehicle already parked
10. Directly at the entrance or exit of a building or driveway, or within 5 meters of a driveway entrance
11. Between a safety zone and the road edge, or within 10 meters from the outermost end of the safety zone on both sides
12. In a confined area
13. Within 15 meters before a bus stop sign and 3 meters beyond the sign
14. Within 3 meters of a mailbox
15. In a manner that obstructs traffic

217.body:
4) Safe Parking Methods
1. Check the rearview mirror to see whether any vehicle is following closely behind. When it is safe, activate the left turn signal to inform following vehicles that you are about to park.
2. Ease off the accelerator and check the side mirror.
3. Observe blind spots and apply the brake.
4. Park close to the left edge of the road, parallel to and no more than 25 centimeters from the road edge or road shoulder, to prevent motorcycles from squeezing into the space between the vehicle and the road edge.
5. Engage the handbrake and shift to neutral for manual transmission, or P for automatic transmission.

5) Parking in an Emergency
If a driver must park in an emergency, the driver must be mindful of safety and strictly follow the steps below:
1. Turn on the emergency flashers to alert other road users so they can take evasive action.
2. Move the vehicle off the traffic surface to avoid obstructing traffic and to prevent accidents that may result from being sideswiped by other vehicles.
3. Place a warning sign or other material at a distance of no less than 20 meters before the point where the vehicle is parked, so that other drivers are informed and can prepare to take evasive action or reduce speed in advance.
4. Report the incident or request assistance from the relevant agencies, for example: Emergency Hotline 191, Highway Police 1193, Central Traffic Police 1197 (for the Bangkok Metropolitan area), etc.

219.section: In summary, the side effects of many types of medication affect the ability to operate vehicles.
219.body:
In summary, the side effects of many types of medication affect the ability to operate vehicles.

• Prescription medications such as sleeping pills, psychiatric medications, all types of neurological medications, and injectable diabetes medication (insulin) often have significant nervous system side effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, blurred vision, double vision, and fatigue—especially anti-seizure medications.

• Those who purchase and take medications on their own, such as common antihistamines, must absolutely refrain from operating vehicles and always bear in mind that the side effects of medication may last up to 24 hours.

• Drivers should avoid taking cough suppressants, stomach pain relievers, and muscle pain relievers/muscle relaxants.

• Drivers who regularly take prescription medications that have side effects causing dizziness or lightheadedness should avoid driving while taking these medications.

**Diseases That Affect Driving**

Because driving requires coping with stressful conditions and sustained concentration over long periods, drivers must be in good physical health. Those with chronic conditions should observe precautions classified by type of disease as follows:

1) **Diabetes** – The risk of accidents often arises from low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). This risk varies according to the severity of the disease. Symptoms may include palpitations, restlessness, nausea, sweating, or feeling hungry—in which case fruit juice or milk should be consumed immediately. If hypoglycemia becomes more severe, it may cause confusion, cold body temperature, memory loss, seizures, loss of consciousness, and death.

   1. Those treated by dietary control alone, if there are no complications from the disease such as diabetic blurred vision, may drive normally.

   2. Those treated with oral medications that do not carry a risk of hypoglycemia may drive normally. Those treated with oral medications in a drug group that carries a risk of hypoglycemia, and who have not experienced episodes of hypoglycemia requiring assistance from others in the past 3–12 months, may drive but must exercise caution, remain aware of hypoglycemia, and check blood sugar levels at least 2 times per day.

   3. Diabetic patients treated with insulin injections must not have experienced episodes of hypoglycemia requiring assistance from others in the past 3–12 months. They may drive but must exercise caution, remain aware of the signs of hypoglycemia, check blood sugar levels at least 2 times per day, and must pass an eye examination. However, drivers who experience hypoglycemia without apparent symptoms should refrain from driving until the condition can be controlled.

In conclusion, diabetic patients should be aware of the symptoms of both mild and severe hypoglycemia. They should take periodic rest breaks while driving and eat snacks, as well as keep sweets within easy reach for when warning signs of hypoglycemia occur. They should follow their doctor's advice and wear a wristband identifying them as diabetic to facilitate prompt assistance in the event of severe hypoglycemia.

222.body:
2.3 Perception of Hazardous Situations

1) Risk Assessment

Accidents are something no one wants to happen, but when they do occur, investigation of accident causes reveals that nearly every accident is preventable. From traffic accident statistics, out of 100 accidents, over 80 fall into 3 types of collisions: rear-end collisions 33 times, intersection collisions 32 times, collisions with roadside objects while driving on curves 8 times, and collisions with roadside objects while driving on straight roads 9 times. Drivers often think these collisions may be due to poor visibility or bad weather conditions. However, most of these incidents occur during daytime under normal weather and visibility conditions. It is certain that they are most commonly found among new drivers, especially when visibility is poor, on secondary roads where road conditions are bad, or where there are many obstructions. It is normal for new drivers to have accidents due to insufficient experience, and they tend to exhibit unsafe driving behaviors such as following the vehicle ahead too closely, driving too fast, misjudging distances when overtaking or passing through intersections, and not observing the road environment ahead well enough. Therefore, it is necessary to know and be aware of these dangers, as well as to learn what should be done for the safety of yourself and other drivers.

2) Avoiding Risky Situations

As a new driver, it is necessary to know what is dangerous and may cause accidents. Practicing on real roads to build experience is absolutely essential. Meanwhile, new drivers lack both maturity and experience, which cannot be built in a short time. Studies from many countries have found that accidents among new drivers can be significantly reduced by building experience through simulating various situations that closely resemble actual road use, whether through computer-based training or through practice and repetition of tests on hazard perception and risk response.

• Speed Control: Driving at high speed is a major cause of accidents among new drivers, as it prevents them from observing surrounding hazards, warning signs, and changing road conditions such as curves, and from responding in time, resulting in accidents. Many drivers may not see the importance of reducing speed even by a small amount. However, in reality, even a slight difference in speed can produce vastly different outcomes when an accident occurs. For example, if you hit a pedestrian at 60 km/h, that person has a high chance of dying, but if the speed is 30 km/h, the person may be injured but the chance of death is significantly reduced.

223.body:
• Safe speed in various situations

What would happen if the vehicle in front of us brakes suddenly? If you maintain too short a following distance to brake and stop in time, an accident will certainly occur. So how much following distance should we maintain to be safe? Generally, a normal person takes no more than 2 seconds to brake, and an additional 1 second is calculated as a safety margin. We can use this to estimate distance by observing when the vehicle ahead passes a tree, then counting 3 seconds in our mind, or counting "one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three" silently. If our vehicle passes the same tree before we finish counting, it means we are following too closely. Slow down and repeat the process until our vehicle passes just as we count to "one thousand three." In cases of poor visibility, such as rain, wet roads, or fog, you may count more than that, such as 4 seconds or "one thousand four."

In addition to maintaining a following distance, speed control is very important, especially when it has just started raining and the road is slippery. Sudden braking can cause the vehicle to skid off the road, collide with another vehicle, or overturn. Therefore, you must reduce speed, avoid sudden braking, or swerving immediately. Drive at a constant speed and maintain a sufficient following distance. If there is dense fog, you should not drive faster than 50 km/h.

For safe driving, maintain a following distance from the vehicle ahead as follows: for every 10 km/h of speed, allow 5 meters of following distance. For example, at a speed of 50 km/h, maintain a following distance of 25 meters. However, in poor weather conditions, the following distance should be increased by at least double. Maintaining such a following distance will help reduce accidents. If you cannot see ahead of the vehicle in front of you, increase the following distance further, because the vehicle ahead may change lanes without reducing speed or stopping, which poses a risk of an accident.

If you need to stop, pull over to the left and use hazard lights. Try to park on the left side or on the road shoulder, otherwise serious damage may occur. If you must park on the road shoulder, turn on hazard lights whether during the day or at night. Also place a warning triangle sign on the vehicle so that it can be used at night—it will help prevent your vehicle from being hit.

224.section: Choose an appropriate speed for safety in various situations
224.body:
At nighttime, severe accidents tend to occur frequently because traffic is lighter than during the daytime, so drivers tend to drive at full speed, resulting in severe accidents at night. Drivers should therefore drive at a speed that allows them to stop within their visible range.

• Choose an appropriate speed for safety in various situations

What is the appropriate speed?

The appropriate speed is a speed that is suitable for the surrounding conditions, road conditions, and does not cause fatalities to others in the event of an accident, or the speed limit indicated on traffic signs as shown in the illustration, which is determined by considering the type of road, the situation, the surrounding conditions, and the recommended safe speed for various types of road users. Therefore, new drivers should drive at the speed specified on traffic signs or at the speed limits prescribed by law, and slow down when approaching curves or when visibility is poor, such as during rain, etc.

225.body:
• Keeping a Side Distance

A side distance of at least approximately 1 meter should be maintained, as other vehicles may open their doors, causing an accident. This distance is also appropriate for avoiding sideswipe collisions with bicycles and motorcycles traveling alongside your vehicle. In addition, vehicles beside you may obstruct various hazards such as pedestrians and motorcycles on the other side.

• Keeping a Distance When Overtaking, Changing Lanes, or at Intersections

This distance refers to the gap between your vehicle and other vehicles on the road, allowing the driver to proceed safely without an accident. If the gap is not large enough, you should stop and wait until that vehicle has passed or until there is a sufficient gap, for safety. If there is not enough distance from oncoming vehicles to make a turn, you should stop and wait until the vehicles have passed or there is a large enough gap.

92

226.body:
• Judging distance when turning
A right turn requires more space—2 lanes—so it can be made at a greater speed than a left turn. A left turn, on the other hand, is easier and shorter than a right turn. You should maintain a distance of approximately 100 meters from an approaching vehicle (count "one thousand one" to "one thousand six" in your mind). Judging distance requires experience and practice. In addition, a precaution to observe is: do not overtake while a large truck is turning, because this type of vehicle may need 2 lanes to complete the turn. Your vehicle may not be able to avoid it, resulting in an accident.

• Turning at a four-way intersection
Turning at a four-way intersection is more difficult than making a regular turn, especially at locations without traffic signals, because you must watch for vehicles from the remaining 3 directions until there is a safe gap. Generally, this gap should be 4–6 seconds (70–100 meters) before proceeding. If you are not confident about the gap, wait until the distance is sufficient or until other vehicles have passed.

228.body:
• Reducing Blind Spots

The skill of reducing blind spots can be easily practiced but is often neglected or not recognized by new drivers. In practice, after undergoing both theoretical training and practical training from experts, this skill is easy to develop and very beneficial for new drivers, who can practice on their own or through experts by following these steps:

1. Look far ahead 200–300 meters and do not fixate on a single point for a long time.
2. Check the various mirrors and inspect blind spots periodically (approximately every 8–10 seconds).
3. Avoid hanging clothes or other items in the rear left seat area of the vehicle.
4. Avoid driving behind large vehicles for extended periods.
5. Increase the following distance from the vehicle ahead.
6. While overtaking, check the side mirror along the vehicle's blind spot by glancing over your shoulder.
7. When reversing, make sure there are no people or obstructions behind the vehicle. Drivers of large vehicles should exercise extra caution to prevent accidents.

In addition, a correct driving posture and proper adjustment of the side mirrors and rearview mirror can greatly reduce blind spots. The rearview mirror must be adjusted so that the entire rear window is visible, allowing you to see vehicles following behind (Figure 1). The side mirrors should be adjusted to see vehicles behind that are about to overtake and vehicles in the lane offset to the rear, adjusted parallel to the body of the vehicle (Figures 2–3).

If you need to change lanes and a vehicle beside you enters the blind spot area, the side mirror will show whether a vehicle is still in the blind spot. If there is none, you may change lanes.

Note: Humans can detect moving objects more easily than stationary ones, such as a car parked on the roadside. Therefore, exercise caution in this regard.

229.section: 3) Case Studies on Risk Assessment of People, Vehicles, and Roads
229.body:
3) Case Studies on Risk Assessment of People, Vehicles, and Roads

Although hazard awareness is important in everyday driving, in certain situations it is critically important for your safety and the safety of other road users, such as bicycles, pedestrians, ambulances, etc. These situations can still be managed by maintaining a sufficient safe following distance, observing hazards, and stopping, reducing speed, or swerving to avoid them.

• **Cyclists** can be found on roads, sidewalks, and bicycle lanes. This group moves back and forth between sidewalks and roads, making them difficult to observe. Although most cyclists are found on roads, this group moves faster than pedestrians but slower than cars, especially when turning at intersections. However, cyclists sometimes do not follow traffic rules, such as riding against traffic or ignoring traffic signals. Therefore, one must consider the possibilities from roads and sidewalks and should maintain a sufficient distance, use the horn, and make eye contact to ensure that the cyclist has noticed your vehicle. In some cases, you may need to stop until it is safe.

• **Motorcycles** — Like other groups, motorcycles are smaller than cars and therefore difficult to see. They often weave quickly and change lanes frequently, especially during heavy traffic, making them difficult to observe and predict. Many times they are obscured by large vehicles such as trucks, buses, or are in your vehicle's blind spot, causing them to appear suddenly and at close range, resulting in accidents. Car drivers often report that they did not notice the motorcycle. Accidents frequently occur while motorcycles are making turns. Therefore, car drivers should exercise caution and check their blind spots, especially when turning, overtaking, or driving through intersections.

• **Pedestrians** are something all drivers greatly fear, as it is a serious matter that can result in severe injuries and possibly death. Therefore, drivers should exercise extra caution when encountering pedestrians crossing the road, typically around department stores, schools, bus stops, and intersections. Drivers must observe the road, sidewalks, and between parked vehicles, especially since small children are difficult to see because they are blocked by other vehicles. Additionally, they may appear suddenly in unexpected areas, such as between parked vehicles. Groups requiring special caution include children and the elderly, as children may dart out quickly, while the elderly may not notice, see, or sense an approaching vehicle and take longer than normal to cross the road. Therefore, you should reduce speed when entering areas where pedestrians are likely to be present, such as schools, department stores, and residential communities. Maintain distance from pedestrians and try to make eye contact to ensure they have seen your vehicle, using the horn when necessary until you have passed through the area. In addition, you should always stop to let people cross. Stopping the vehicle will prevent people from running across in front of your car. When approaching an intersection, slow down. If your vehicle is in the far-left or far-right lane, check whether anyone is about to cross the road. If so, stop and wait for them to cross. Drivers often worry about being rear-ended by the vehicle behind them. Therefore, you should signal to the vehicle following behind before slowing down. Drive at a steady pace and do not accelerate frequently, as this will require more braking, which can confuse the vehicle behind you.

233.section: Case of a car door being suddenly opened
233.body:
• Case of a car door being suddenly opened
Observation: Observe the vehicle ahead that is parking—whether there are people inside the vehicle or not.
Anticipation: The door may be opened without caution.
Correction: Be cautious, alert, and prepared.
• Use an appropriate speed.
• Maintain a distance of no less than 1 meter from vehicles parked in a row.
• Use the horn as a warning if suspicious or unsure.
Always remember that when driving in a community area, this kind of situation can occur at any time. Being prepared and alert is essential.

• Case of a vehicle suddenly pulling out from a parking spot
Observation: Observe the vehicle ahead that is parking—whether there are people inside the vehicle or not.
Anticipation: The vehicle may pull out without signaling and without checking behind.
Correction: Be cautious, alert, and prepared.
• Use an appropriate speed.
• Maintain a distance of no less than 1 meter from vehicles parked in a row.
• Use the horn as a warning if suspicious or unsure.
When driving into a community area or driving near department stores, public parks, or fresh markets, this kind of situation can occur at any time. Always remember that you must use only low speed in community areas.

• Case of a vehicle reversing out of a house onto the road or out of a side street (soi) onto the road
Observation: Observe the entrance of the side street or the driveway—whether there is a vehicle or not.
Anticipation: A vehicle may drive out without signaling, without slowing down, and without looking left and right.
Correction: Be cautious, alert, and prepared.
• Use an appropriate speed.
• Maintain a distance of no less than 1 meter from vehicles parked in a row.
• Use the horn as a warning if suspicious or unsure.
When driving into a community area or driving near department stores, public parks, or fresh markets, this kind of situation can occur at any time. Always remember that you must use only low speed in community areas.

234.body:
• Case of a vehicle cutting in front, people and animals crossing the road at close range, or a bus stopping at the roadside

**Observation**
- Observe the behavior of the vehicle ahead.
- Observe people standing at the roadside.

**Anticipation**
- A vehicle may cut in front.
- People may get off the vehicle and walk across in front of your vehicle.

**Corrective Action / Guidelines**
- Reduce speed.
- Sound the horn as a warning at an appropriate distance.
- If there is still no response, warn again.
- If there is still no response, reduce speed and prepare to stop the vehicle.

• Case of driving at night when the vehicle ahead has no tail lights

**Observation / Corrective Action:** Stay alert at all times.

**Anticipation:** There may be a vehicle traveling on the road or at the roadside without tail lights.

**Guidelines**
- Exercise caution.
- Do not drive fast.
- Drive at a speed that allows you to stop within the distance illuminated by your headlights and where visibility is clear.

237.body:
• Driving through rain/water
- Use low speed to prevent water from splashing onto pedestrians or other vehicles.
- Avoid road surfaces with standing water, as they may cause skidding and splashing.
- Do not turn on emergency flashers while it is raining, as this will annoy and distract drivers following behind, and it is also a violation of traffic rules.
- Maintain a sufficient distance from the vehicle ahead, at least twice the distance used on dry roads, because brakes may be more slippery than under normal conditions, so as not to frighten the vehicle ahead into accelerating away from you.

• Stopping the vehicle
- Check the rearview mirror to see whether any vehicle is following behind.
- Give a signal in advance at an appropriate distance, whether by tapping the brake lights as a warning or signaling with the left turn indicator.
- Reduce speed by gradually tapping the brakes at a distance that allows the vehicle behind enough time to brake in time.
- Do not stop the vehicle blocking entrances/exits, blocking the "Left Turn Through at All Times" lane, blocking the "Diagonal Lines – No Stopping" (เส้นทแยงห้ามหยุด) area, or obstructing traffic. If your parked vehicle blocks another vehicle, you must find a way to move your vehicle to clear the way for others.

• Using the brakes
- Do not tap the brakes unnecessarily or too frequently, as this will annoy the vehicle following behind, which must also brake unnecessarily in response.
- Brake lights should be inspected regularly.

• Parking
- Do not park in no-parking zones.
- Park as close to the curb as possible.
- Do not park blocking the entrance/exit of other people's buildings or residences. If it is necessary, set the wheels straight, do not engage the handbrake, and leave the gear in neutral.
- If parking for a long period, turn off the engine.

• Parking in designated parking spaces
- Reverse into the parking space with the front of the vehicle facing out, and park parallel and straight within the parking space. Do not park straddling the parking lines or too close to the lines so that other vehicles cannot park.
- Check the distance between vehicles to allow other vehicles to park conveniently and open their doors easily.
- Do not double-park. However, if it is necessary to double-park, set the wheels straight, do not engage the handbrake or lock the gear, so that others can push your vehicle out and allow the vehicle parked on the inside to drive out.

• Using a telephone while driving
The behavior of using a telephone while driving is considered a new behavior of people in this era. It requires cultivating awareness that drivers are not only responsible for their own lives and the lives of passengers in the vehicle, but must also be responsible for the lives of others on the road.

238.body:
# Recommended Practices for Safe Driving

1. If driving a short distance and the travel time to the destination is not long, you should not use the phone to open or reply to messages until you reach your destination. If driving a long distance that takes a long time, you should designate rest stops, such as stopping every one hour, and make phone calls when you reach the rest stop.

2. You should park on the roadside in a safe location before using the phone. If you are in heavy traffic or must continue driving, you should drive close to the left and slow down, and have hands-free accessories ready for use when starting a conversation.

3. You should inform the person you are speaking with that you are driving, and keep the conversation as brief as possible.

4. Avoid conversation topics that cause sadness, anger, irritation, or emotional distress.

5. Do not receive or send text messages (SMS) or emails under any circumstances.

6. Before driving, plan to turn off all communication channels that may disturb your driving.

• **Driving Through Crossings in Community Areas or School Zones**
Reduce speed and exercise more caution than usual. Be courteous to pedestrians crossing the road. Do not honk the horn or flash lights in a manner that chases or startles them.

• **Maintaining Distance from the Vehicle Ahead**
It is important not to tailgate the vehicle ahead, as it can cause accidents. Rear-end collisions in Thailand often involve multiple vehicles at once—sometimes over ten vehicles in a chain collision at certain locations. As speed increases, the following distance from the vehicle ahead must also increase accordingly, including the legal consequences that follow. The vehicle following behind must maintain sufficient distance from the vehicle ahead to be able to stop safely when the vehicle ahead is involved in an accident or stops suddenly. If you are following and rear-end the vehicle ahead, it clearly means you are at fault.

• **Accelerating**
Accelerating to high speeds in a manner that causes passengers in the vehicle to feel afraid, or causes other road users to feel startled and anticipate a possible accident, is something drivers must refrain from or avoid. Always exercise caution in maintaining an appropriate speed relative to other vehicles sharing the road. For example, suddenly swerving out of a lane to overtake may cause a collision with oncoming vehicles traveling in their normal lane. Tailgating the vehicle ahead, flashing lights to force the vehicle ahead to give way, or honking to chase them may provoke the emotions of other drivers. There have been many news reports of drivers on the road chasing and shooting at each other. Most importantly, this may cause accidents involving other vehicles on the road.

• **Slowing Down**
Slow down, and whichever vehicle reaches the intersection or junction first has the right to proceed first. If vehicles arrive at the intersection or junction at the same time, the vehicle on the left goes first. In the case of a major road and minor road, vehicles on the minor road must always stop and yield to vehicles on the major road. How do you know which is the major road and which is the minor road? Observe the traffic signs. If the vehicle ahead drives with an excessively large gap while the road ahead is clear, it wastes road surface capacity, and if many people do this, it will affect road usage. Driving with an excessively large gap has more negative effects than one might think, because the vehicle behind will try to overtake, increasing the chance of side-swipe or collision accidents.

239.body:
• Yielding the right of way
You must yield to vehicles from the right when driving to an intersection, junction, or roundabout. Most people do not know that they must yield to vehicles from the right when arriving at a major intersection, whether a three-way or four-way intersection without traffic signals, including when entering a roundabout—you must always yield to vehicles from the right. Since Thailand drives on the left lane, when reaching an intersection or roundabout where a vehicle is coming from the right, that vehicle is considered to have arrived first. Therefore, you must always reduce speed and ensure it is safe before proceeding. When entering a main road, such as when driving on a frontage road and intending to merge right into the main lane, you must slow down and let vehicles traveling straight go first.

• Do not stay in the right lane
On roads with more than two lanes, you should not stay in the right lane, even if you are driving at the speed prescribed by law. On an open road, no matter how fast you are driving, you should not stay in the right lane. Many times on roads with heavy traffic moving slowly, when you cannot weave through gaps to get ahead, you find a vehicle staying in the right lane at a constant speed—possibly at the legal speed limit—but causing a long queue of vehicles behind. Therefore, whether the road is clear or not, whether driving slowly or fast, you should drive in the middle lane or the second lane from the rightmost lane. Always keep in mind that if you are in the right lane and a vehicle comes up behind you, it means you are driving too slowly. As a matter of courtesy, you should activate your left turn signal and move aside to let the vehicle behind pass. Many times, those unaware of proper etiquette become irritated and accuse the vehicle behind of flashing high beams at them. Always remember that the right lane is the lane for overtaking or changing lanes for vehicles traveling faster.

• Signaling
Using the horn signal: The horn is meant to be used as a warning or caution that an accident may occur, using short honks—not long honks, as that resembles scolding or criticizing other drivers. Do not use the horn in community areas, hospitals, or no-honking zones. Do not use the horn while the vehicle is parked, unless another vehicle is reversing toward you. You should sound the horn when driving on a curve where you cannot see oncoming vehicles, at blind corners in alleys with solid walls blocking the view, or in areas where you are unsure, to warn oncoming vehicles. In emergencies, such as brake failure or a tire blowout, sound the horn to alert other vehicles so they can take evasive action. Use the horn when you need to call for help. Hand signals: To express gratitude or apology, raise your hand to show thanks for being given way, or raise your hand to show an apology, with the hand raised to ear level and a slight bow of the head—for example, when given way to overtake or merge into a lane.

• Normal driving
Always drive close to the left side of the road or in the left lane, especially when driving slowly, as it obstructs other vehicles. Do not straddle lanes. Do not use high beams. Apply the brakes only when necessary so that the vehicle behind does not have to brake abruptly. When changing lanes, always signal beforehand. Give way to emergency vehicles. Do not tailgate; maintain an appropriate distance from the vehicle ahead.

240.body:
• Driving in Opposite Directions
On roads where vehicles travel in both directions, if there is an oncoming vehicle, you must reduce speed, use an appropriate speed, and keep as far left as possible to prevent accidents or close calls. Do not use high beams, as they will dazzle the driver of the oncoming vehicle. Keep as close to the left edge of the road as possible and do not straddle lanes into other traffic lanes.

• Moving a Vehicle from a Parked Position
The driver must always signal before moving the vehicle from a parked position. Check the rearview mirror or side mirrors, and only pull out from the parking space when it is safe to do so. Press the accelerator gently and smoothly; do not jerk the vehicle forward or pull out onto the road in a manner that forces other drivers to swerve or brake suddenly.

• Overtaking Another Vehicle
- Before overtaking another vehicle, you must always signal before overtaking.
- Flash the headlights briefly 2 times so that the driver of the vehicle ahead can see and know that someone wishes to overtake.
- Do not overtake in a no-overtaking zone. If the road is narrow, drive slowly and overtake with caution.
- Maintain an appropriate distance from the vehicle being overtaken. After overtaking, do not cut back into the left lane too quickly, as this may cause a collision with the vehicle being overtaken.
- Once you have completely passed the other vehicle, immediately move back into the left traffic lane.

242.body:
• Changing Lanes
- A driver who wishes to change lanes must signal with the left or right turn indicator, as applicable, in advance at an appropriate distance, or at least 30 meters before changing lanes.
- Do not change lanes at a critical or dangerously close distance.
- Change lanes carefully only when it is confirmed safe to do so.
- Return the turn signal to its normal position.
- Adjust speed to match the traffic in the lane being entered.
- Be careful not to cause following vehicles to stop abruptly or brake unexpectedly.

• Using Turn Signals
Failure to signal when stopping, slowing down, or turning causes more than 700 accidents per year. Simply using the turn signal can prevent these accidents. The benefits of using turn signals are as follows:
- To inform fellow road users of the direction we intend to go or to request to overtake.
- Using the left or right turn signal to indicate the desired turning direction.
- When making a U-turn, changing lanes, overtaking another vehicle, or pulling out of a parking space.
- Proper use of turn signals: When turning or overtaking, the driver must activate the turn signal at the front or side of the vehicle so that the amber flashing signal light at the rear of the vehicle indicates the same direction as the intended turn or lane change.
- The turn signal should be activated clearly enough for the vehicle behind to see before turning. In terms of speed, if traveling at 30 km/h, activate the turn signal at least 30 meters in advance; if traveling at 60 km/h, activate the turn signal at least 60 meters in advance.
- We should make it a habit to use turn signals, even when there are no vehicles following behind.
- When turning at a U-turn point, upon reaching the turning point, activate the turn signal, slow down, and then change lanes.
- When turning into or out of a side street (soi), also check for traffic from the right and exercise caution before turning. In the case of motorcycles, before reaching an intersection where a turn is intended, the turn signal should be activated at least 30 meters before the intersection so that following drivers can see that we are about to turn and can prepare in time.

• Sharing the Road with Motorcycles
- Do not tailgate the vehicle in front.
- Press the accelerator gently so as not to frighten passengers in the vehicle or cause other road users to feel afraid of an accident occurring.
- When there is flooding, use low speed to prevent water from splashing onto pedestrians or other vehicles.
- Check the rearview mirror to see if there are vehicles following behind. Signal in advance at an appropriate distance, whether it is the brake light or left turn signal, and reduce speed gradually.
- Slow down, and whichever vehicle arrives at the intersection first has the right of way. If vehicles arrive at the intersection at the same time, the vehicle on the left should be given the right of way.
- On roads with more than two lanes, do not stay in the right lane, as this will obstruct other vehicles that wish to overtake.

243.body:
• Sharing the Road with Bicycles
- Check blind spots every time. There may be bicycles riding along the roadside or coming from the opposite direction.
- When entering or exiting lanes in community areas or public parks, exercise caution as cyclists may be passing in and out.

• Using Expressways and Special Highways
Expressways and special highways differ from ordinary roads because they are designed for certain types of vehicles and allow higher speeds with greater safety. When driving on expressways and special highways, the following must be known:

1. You must hold a driving license matching the type of vehicle. Learner drivers should not drive on expressways or highways.
2. You must know the various traffic signs, warning signals, etc.
3. You must be ready and alert while driving at all times throughout the journey.
4. You should not use the expressway if you feel fatigued, drowsy, or unwell.
5. When fatigued or exhausted, you should rest before traveling.
6. Stopping or parking is prohibited except in an emergency, and you must park close to the road edge.
7. Certain types of vehicles are prohibited from using expressways and special highways.
8. You must ensure that your vehicle is in good condition and safe to drive.

• Speed Limits on Expressways and Special Highways
The speed permitted on expressways or special highways, according to the Road Traffic Act B.E. 2522, designates Special Highway No. 7 (Motorway) and Special Highway No. 9 (Kanchanaphisek Ring Road) with a maximum speed limit of 120 kilometers/hour. Therefore, expressways and special highways that are not the Motorway or Kanchanaphisek Ring Road must comply with the legal speed limits referenced for areas within/outside municipal zones, which are no more than 80 and 90 kilometers/hour, respectively.

• Route Guide Signs and Expressway Public Relations Signs
Overhead Signs are green signs installed at an elevated level above head height to guide routes on the expressway at intervals before each expressway exit at distances of 1,000 meters, 500 meters, and at the exit area, so that users can prepare and enter the correct lane to reach their destination.

• Speed Limit and Emergency Lane Closure Signs (Matrix Sign)
These are signal signs installed along the median of the expressway at intervals. The information displayed on these signs mostly consists of numbers indicating the recommended speed on the expressway at that time, such as in cases of rain or dense fog, etc. In addition, they display symbols indicating whether traffic lanes are open or closed, in order to inform or warn users in advance when there is an accident or road maintenance.

• Variable Message Sign (VMS)
This is an electronic sign that provides various information to users, mostly reporting traffic conditions on the expressway or providing recommendations to users. These signs are installed near the area before tollgate entrances and on the expressway.

244.body:
• Cooperating with Emergency Vehicles

Cooperating with or yielding the right of way to emergency vehicles is something that the general public should be aware of and cooperate with by clearing the way. In the case of emergency ambulances that need to request the right of way using flashing lights and sirens in order to transport patients for timely medical treatment, you should promptly make way for such ambulances as if your own family members were experiencing a medical emergency and urgently needed help. This also helps prevent accidents involving those ambulances. In addition to helping emergency vehicles travel to pick up or transport emergency patients to the hospital quickly and safely, this is also in compliance with the Road Traffic Act B.E. 2522, Section 76, which stipulates that when a driver sees a fire truck or ambulance performing its duties with flashing light signals, the driver must stop or park the vehicle close to the left edge of the road as quickly as possible and must exercise due caution as appropriate. Anyone who violates this shall be guilty of an offense and subject to penalties as prescribed by law.

• Expressing Gratitude

Expressing gratitude is an etiquette that must be practiced until it becomes a habit. In cases where we receive good treatment or goodwill from fellow road users—such as being allowed to merge into a traffic lane, being given way to overtake, or being warned by oncoming vehicles that there is a police checkpoint ahead—we should express gratitude by bowing the head in thanks, giving a smile of thanks, or raising the right hand while bowing the head, etc.

• Expressing an Apology

In cases where we drive with poor etiquette, violate traffic rules, or do anything that causes inconvenience to others, we must not neglect to express an apology by raising the right hand to eyebrow level while bowing the head, or by other gestures that convey that we are aware of our mistake and are sorry. This is because such situations may lead to accidents, retaliation from those affected, or altercations on the road.

• Forgiveness

Forgiving others while driving is essential to keeping the driver calm and preventing feelings of irritation, anger, or hot-headedness when others commit driving discourtesies that affect the smooth flow of our driving. For example, if someone cuts into our traffic lane causing us to brake suddenly, we should forgive them by not flashing our lights or honking the horn at them when we see that person express an apology.

• Sharing Goodwill

Sharing goodwill is something that is absolutely necessary while driving on the road, because in addition to making the journey smooth, it also makes the driver who shows goodwill feel at ease and less stressed about the journey. Sharing goodwill through kindness toward pedestrians includes: being careful not to splash water on pedestrians, stopping to let pedestrians cross the road, and not honking the horn to startle them. Showing goodwill toward other drivers includes: allowing them to merge into the traffic lane, giving way for overtaking, warning oncoming vehicles that there is a police checkpoint ahead, and most importantly, not bearing grudges against others and knowing how to forgive others. For example, if someone cuts into the traffic lane we are using, causing us to brake suddenly, we should forgive them by not flashing our lights or honking the horn at them, etc.

245.body:
At present, driving vehicles on public roads requires more than just strict compliance with traffic laws alone—it is not sufficient. This is because some accidents stem from altercations caused by a lack of driving etiquette awareness. Therefore, drivers should collectively exercise good awareness, good manners, and goodwill toward fellow road users, adhering to a simple principle: **"4 Prohibitions, 2 Musts"**

**4 Prohibitions:**

**1. Do not drive fast**

For driving on urban roads or highways, the speed limit is set at no more than 80 kilometers per hour. For driving on rural highways (inter-provincial highways), cars or motorcycles must not exceed 90 kilometers per hour.

**2. Do not drink and drive**

According to the Notification of the Office of the Prime Minister regarding Designation of Places or Areas Prohibiting the Consumption of Alcoholic Beverages on Roads, B.E. 2555 (2012), Clause 1: No person shall consume alcoholic beverages on a road while driving or while riding in or on a vehicle.

The terms "road" and "vehicle" under the first paragraph shall have the meanings of "road" and "vehicle" as defined under the law on road traffic.

**3. Do not call and drive**

The Road Traffic Act, B.E. 2522 (1979), Section 43(9), stipulates that drivers are prohibited from using a telephone or any other communication device while the vehicle is in motion, except for the use of a mobile phone with a hands-free accessory for conversation whereby the driver does not have to hold or grip the mobile phone, such as a SmallTalk or Bluetooth device. Violators are subject to a fine of 400–1,000 baht.

Using a phone in cases of traffic congestion or at a red light is also considered an offense in all cases, whether it involves dialing a number, answering a call, playing games, viewing or typing messages, viewing images, or any other activity the phone is capable of, because the person is still considered to be driving—the engine is still running and the driver must still be in control of the vehicle. If anyone needs to use a phone, they should pull over to the side of the road in an area where parking is permitted or stop at a gas station, complete their phone business, and then return to the road. Alternatively, they may use hands-free accessories for phone conversations, such as Bluetooth earphones, or place the phone down and use the speakerphone. However, it is prohibited to talk on the phone by clamping it between the neck or having someone else hold it.

As for other behaviors involving mobile phones, besides talking on the phone and chatting, viewing any information from the internet via a mobile phone is also an offense. This includes using a stand to mount the phone on the steering wheel for phone use, which also constitutes an offense because it greatly disturbs concentration while driving, as the driver must take their eyes off the road and also take their hands off the steering wheel to tap the screen.

**4. Do not drive when drowsy**

The primary cause of falling asleep at the wheel that everyone thinks of is sleep deprivation. Insufficient rest causes some drivers to overlook this and fail to take precautions, making it one of the leading causes of road accidents worldwide. Drowsiness while driving can occur in any driver—those who are sleep-deprived, those who have accumulated insufficient rest over a prolonged period causing the body's internal clock and work/life schedules to be out of sync, those who take medications that cause drowsiness such as cold medicine or allergy medication, those who consume alcoholic beverages, as well as those with underlying medical conditions and abnormal sleep disorders that have not been treated, such as narcolepsy, snoring, and sleep apnea. These are additional factors that cause many drivers to feel drowsy and groggy at all times, even when they have had sufficient rest.
